strengths: Introduces a large-scale 5G observability dataset with over 1M observations at 100ms resolution, 18 heterogeneous KPIs (10 float, 6 integer, 2 categorical), de-anonymized scale information, and multiple scenarios including YouTube/Twitch/file download, mobility, congestion, and jamming.

Provides a multi-task benchmark spanning anomaly detection, anomaly duration localization, root cause analysis, forecasting, and question answering, with real jamming anomalies and ten synthetic anomaly types grounded in telecom literature and expert review.

Data collection is described in substantial detail (OpenAirInterface 5G stack, USRP N300/X310, zones A/B/C, KL-divergence/histogram-based synchronization, KPI definitions), supporting the realism and operational relevance of the dataset.

Benchmarks a diverse set of models, including GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, Moment, Moirai2, Toto, Mantis, TimesNet, Autoformer, and others, and identifies practical failure modes such as high false-positive rates and missed peaks in forecasting.

The scale-information analysis, especially the strong performance of Mantis and Toto, provides a useful hypothesis for time series foundation model design: preserving absolute scale and pretraining on observability-like data matters.
The anomaly curation includes principled transformations with soft bounds, noise injection, and human-verified troubleshooting tickets, going beyond naive random perturbations.
weaknesses: Dataset availability and reproducibility are not documented: no URL, license, datasheet, access instructions, code, or exact split/seed details. This is critical for a dataset contribution and prevents others from reliably building on it.

The model comparison is not apples-to-apples: LLMs and reasoning models are evaluated zero-shot, while time series models and foundation models have trained classification/regression heads. Thus the claim that state-of-the-art approaches struggle is confounded by adaptation and training differences.

Evaluation is statistically underpowered: anomaly detection uses only 1,000 samples (about 50 anomalies), and no confidence intervals, error bars, or repeated runs are reported, so small differences may be noise.

The anomaly tasks mix real jamming and synthetic anomalies, but results are not disaggregated by anomaly source, so it is unclear whether models are learning real fault signatures or synthetic artifacts.

QA evaluation is incomplete: only LLMs are tested, Table 6 reports only best/worst KPI for statistics and periodicity rather than aggregate performance, the jammer question from the prompt is missing from the table, and GPT-4.1-generated QA templates lack clear human validation.

Forecasting metrics are not clearly normalized, and aggregate MAE/RMSE may be dominated by zero or stable periods. Despite claims about spikes and peak failures, there is no peak-focused or per-KPI error analysis.

The paper lacks a limitations section and broader impact/ethics discussion, omitting important caveats about the single-base-station lab setup, limited mobility/congestion scenarios, synthetic anomaly realism, and applicability to cloud/IT observability.

The scope is narrower than the framing: observability is represented only by a controlled 5G lab network, not enterprise cloud/IT systems; the claim of de-anonymized covariates applies to this lab trace, not to proprietary operational data.

Baseline training details are insufficient: classification-head architecture, hyperparameters per model, fine-tuning decisions, prompt parsing, and compute are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility.

Dataset statistics are unclear in places, for example QnA Types: Time Series QA 64, Network QA 5 likely counts templates or questions rather than samples, and no datasheet or per-KPI distribution/quality analysis is provided.

strengths: Addresses a real gap: observability time series are underrepresented in public benchmarks, and TelecomTS provides de-anonymized, scale-preserving, heterogeneous 5G KPIs rather than normalized/anonymized metrics.

The data collection setup is unusually detailed: a standalone OpenAirInterface 5G network, controlled zones, mobility, congestion, application-level traffic, and over-the-air jamming are described, with appendix-level implementation details.

The dataset supports multiple downstream tasks beyond forecasting, including anomaly detection, anomaly duration localization, root-cause/anomaly-type classification, and time-series/network QA, which is more comprehensive than many forecasting-only benchmarks.

The anomaly curation methodology is more principled than random perturbation: it maps ten documented network anomalies to affected KPIs and function classes, and provides prompts and ticket-generation details in the appendix.

The experiments span LLMs, reasoning models, time-series foundation models, and classical TS architectures, which helps expose the difficulty of the data and provides a useful starting point for future benchmarking.
weaknesses: The central claim that preserving absolute scale is crucial is not adequately supported. Mantis performs well, but Mantis is a scale-aware classification foundation model, not a controlled scale ablation; no experiment trains the same model with and without scale information. Moreover, the forecasting MAE/RMSE values (e.g., MAE ~0.14) are implausible for raw KPIs with ranges up to 450M, suggesting the forecasting evaluation likely normalizes or scales the series, which contradicts the paper's scale-preservation narrative.

The anomaly-detection evaluation is not convincing. The test set is 95% normal/5% anomalous, but training is balanced and there is no threshold calibration, validation-based operating point, or AUC/PR-AUC. A trivial all-positive classifier would obtain recall 1.0 and F1 around 0.095, yet several LLMs score near that level. The reported F1 values therefore do not cleanly support the conclusion that models fail because of observability dynamics.

The QA benchmark is largely algorithmic (mean, variance, periodicity, trend) and is evaluated only with LLMs. A simple calculator or programmatic baseline would solve these questions perfectly; LLM failures may reflect arithmetic limitations rather than time-series understanding. The network QA results are also not compared to class-prior/majority baselines despite severe label imbalance (e.g., only 30k in-motion observations out of 1.14M), making accuracies such as 98.3% potentially trivial or misleading.

The dataset splits and potential leakage are not described. Appendix F says an 80-20 split is used, but the anomaly construction slices sequences with stride 32, so overlapping windows from the same trace may appear in both training and test sets. Grouping by collection session/trace is not discussed, which threatens validity for anomaly detection, root-cause analysis, and duration localization.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a dataset paper. There is no dataset URL, DOI, license, datasheet, download instructions, or code release statement. The paper also does not specify random seeds, exact split files, or preprocessing code, so others cannot reliably reproduce the benchmark results.

The synthetic anomalies and GPT-4.1-generated troubleshooting tickets are not validated quantitatively. 'Human-in-the-loop' verification is mentioned but no annotation protocol, agreement, or error rate is reported. Using GPT-4.1 to generate tickets/QA templates while also evaluating GPT-4.1 raises circularity/contamination concerns that are not addressed.

The root-cause analysis task is really anomaly-type classification over synthetic labels, not root-cause analysis. There is no causal modeling, topology, or system-level reasoning, so the task name overstates what is measured. No simple feature-based or majority-class baselines are provided for comparison.

The data is collected from a single lab-scale 5G base station with three zones and a few applications. This is useful for telecom RAN observability, but it is much narrower than the cloud/IT observability motivation in the introduction, and the paper's claims about general observability data are not fully supported by this setup.

The forecasting evaluation is weak: no input/horizon details, no normalization description, no naive/seasonal-naive baselines, and only MAE/RMSE. The authors themselves note that stable periods inflate MAE/RMSE and mask peak-forecasting failures, yet they do not report peak-specific or scale-normalized metrics.

The paper lacks a limitations section, broader-impact discussion, and dataset datasheet. It does not discuss synthetic-data bias, lab-to-production generalization, potential misuse of de-anonymized network KPIs, or maintenance/licensing plans.

Presentation quality is uneven: inconsistent decimal precision in tables, duplicate or incorrect references (e.g., [41] and [42] appear to be the same work), ambiguous use of 'samples' vs. 'observations', and several grammatical/typographical issues ('covariates' used as singular, 'Q&A' formatting, figure references). These make the paper harder to evaluate and reproduce.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: observability time series are underrepresented in public benchmarks, and TelecomTS provides a de-anonymized, scale-preserving, high-resolution dataset with heterogeneous numerical and categorical KPIs.

The dataset is large and well documented: over 1M observations, 18 KPIs, 100 ms sampling, controlled 5G lab setup, jamming-induced real anomalies, synthetic anomalies grounded in telecom literature, and troubleshooting tickets.

The benchmark is broad and informative across LLMs, reasoning models, time series foundation models, and classic time series architectures, covering anomaly detection, anomaly duration, root-cause analysis, forecasting, and question answering.

The experiments surface useful failure modes: false positives on bursty but normal observability data, poor peak forecasting, difficulty linking temporal and textual context, and sensitivity to absolute scale.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including KPI definitions, anomaly-generation functions, prompts, and training setup, which supports reproducibility if the dataset and splits are released.
Ethical concerns appear limited: the data comes from a lab 5G network rather than private customer traffic, payload data is discarded, and de-anonymization does not expose personal information.
weaknesses: Generalizability is limited. The data comes from a single lab 5G base station with controlled traffic, a small number of devices, and manually defined zones. This is narrower than production observability systems, and real anomalies are only jamming events, while most anomalies are synthetic transformations.

The benchmark comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. LLMs and reasoning models are evaluated zero-shot via prompting, whereas time series models and foundation models are equipped with trained classification or regression heads. Poor LLM performance may therefore reflect the absence of task-specific training rather than only the difficulty of observability data.

The central claim about preserving absolute scale is not directly ablated. Mantis and Toto perform better, but architecture, pretraining data, task head, and normalization choices are confounded. A controlled experiment normalizing inputs for the same model would be needed to isolate the effect of scale.

Synthetic anomaly generation uses GPT-4.1 and handcrafted transformation functions, which may introduce artifacts or unrealistic patterns. Evaluating LLMs on GPT-generated tickets or labels also risks circularity, and the real-anomaly coverage remains narrow.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, seed variance, or repeated runs, and the anomaly detection evaluation uses only 1,000 samples. Prompt sensitivity is not analyzed, despite the heavy reliance on prompt-based LLM evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. There is no explicit dataset URL, license, datasheet, or access procedure, and exact train/test splits and API model configurations are not fully specified. The exact number of Q&A pairs is also unclear from the reported template counts.

Forecasting metrics are hard to interpret because it is unclear whether MAE/RMSE are computed on normalized or original scales. If absolute scale is preserved, errors across heterogeneous KPIs are not directly comparable. Several strong time series foundation baselines, such as Chronos or TimesFM, are not included.

The question-answering benchmark is underdescribed: it is unclear how many total QA examples exist, how they are balanced, and whether GPT-generated question templates introduce leakage or limited diversity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap by introducing TelecomTS, a large-scale 5G observability dataset with de-anonymized, absolute-scale, heterogeneous KPIs and categorical covariates. It fills a real need for public observability benchmarks and supports anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and multi-modal QA.

The data collection pipeline is unusually detailed and well documented: a real standalone 5G network (OpenAirInterface, USRP SDR), 18 KPIs at 100ms resolution, controlled zones, mobility, congestion, and over-the-air jamming, with careful timestamp synchronization via KL divergence. Appendix B provides substantial reproducibility detail.

The task suite is broad and multi-modal: anomaly detection, anomaly duration, root cause analysis, time series QA, network-level QA, and explicit reasoning traces. The dataset is large (32k samples, 2.2M QA instances) and includes both real (jamming) and synthetic anomalies.

The scale ablation in Table 7 provides useful evidence that absolute scale matters: adding an NME branch improves multiple architectures substantially (e.g., Informer anomaly F1 0.451→0.852; Autoformer traffic accuracy 0.578→0.989). This supports the paper's central motivation for scale-aware models.

The benchmark covers a wide range of model families—LLMs, reasoning models, time series foundation models, standard TS architectures, and a multi-modal Toto+Qwen model—and demonstrates practical challenges of erratic, zero-inflated observability data.

Appendix A contrasts TelecomTS with standard benchmarks (UCR, ETTh1, MotorImagery, FRED-MD, Weather, etc.) and clearly illustrates its distinctive heterogeneity, fine-grained resolution, and categorical variables.
weaknesses: Reproducibility and access are seriously under-specified: the manuscript says 'The code is available at:' but provides no URL, and there is no dataset hosting, license, or versioning information. Evaluation details such as random seeds, confidence intervals, exact evaluation set sizes, and hyperparameter search protocols are largely missing.

Claims about the reasoning traces are unsupported. Appendix F.2 states that reasoning traces are validated by 'performance gains observed when models are trained with reasoning (Section 4),' but the reasoning-enabled variant (Toto+Qwen+Thinking) is consistently worse than the non-reasoning variant across tasks (e.g., root cause 0.826→0.720; anomaly detection F1 0.487→0.469; time series QA MAE worse in all categories; network QA worse in all reported columns). No evidence of gains is shown.

The main benchmark tables are selective and inconsistent. Tables 2 and 4 report base (scale-unaware) standard TS models, while Table 7 shows that the same models with NME scale achieve much higher performance (e.g., Informer anomaly F1 0.451→0.852; TimesNet 0.462→0.740). The abstract's claim that 'existing approaches struggle' is therefore overstated without including scale-aware variants in the main comparison. Table 6 reports Toto+Qwen location accuracy 0.400, while Table 7 shows standard TS models with scale achieving >0.9 on 'Location'; the relationship between these evaluations is unclear.

Evaluation methodology has several flaws: anomaly detection uses only 1,000 samples with a balanced 80-20 prevalence rather than natural prevalence, and no confidence intervals are reported. Time series QA reports only best/worst KPI MAE, hiding average performance and mixing incomparable scales (e.g., MAE 3e-4 vs 8569). Network QA omits jammer-presence despite listing five network-level categories. The '64 time series QA categories' in Table 1 is inconsistent with the three task types actually reported. The forecasting table is mislabeled 'accuracy' when reporting MAE/RMSE.

The scale ablation confounds scale information with additional model capacity. The scale-aware variant adds a parallel NME branch and concatenates it with pooled features; no parameter-matched control or alternative scale injection (e.g., raw unnormalized inputs, other normalization schemes) is compared. Thus the improvement cannot be attributed solely to absolute scale.

Dataset generalizability and anomaly realism are not adequately validated. All data come from a single lab 5G testbed with limited hardware and topology, yet the paper claims generalizability beyond the testbed without empirical support. Real anomalies are limited to controlled jamming in Zone A; most anomalies are synthetic transformations generated with GPT-4.1 and sampled parameter ranges, which may not reflect real fault distributions. There is no dedicated limitations section discussing these issues.

Many QA pairs are template-generated statistical extraction (mean, variance, periodicity, trend) and may not require multi-modal reasoning. Reasoning traces are LLM-generated with automatic scoring and no human validation, risking artifacts or hallucinated justifications despite metadata leakage checks. The reported 2.2M QA instances likely contain substantial redundancy.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: observability datasets are scarce, and the few public ones (e.g., BOOM) are anonymized and normalized, removing covariate identity and absolute scale. TelecomTS provides de-anonymized 5G KPIs (18 channels, 32K samples of length 128) with mixed integer/float/categorical covariates and preserved absolute scale, which is a useful artifact for the observability community.

The dataset design is broad: it includes real anomalies induced by a controlled jammer plus synthetic anomalies grounded in telecom literature, and instantiates a suite of downstream tasks (anomaly detection, duration estimation, root cause analysis, forecasting, time-series and network-level QA) with structured metadata and reasoning traces.

Documentation is thorough: appendices cover the 5G testbed, KPI definitions and ranges, trace-alignment via histogram/KL matching, anomaly-curation functions, and all prompts, which substantially aids reproducibility of the data-construction pipeline.

The scale ablation, if reliable, provides practically relevant evidence that magnitude information (mean/std via an NME branch) improves several downstream tasks, and the comparison against Mantis with/without scaling is a reasonable probe of scale sensitivity.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency undermines the headline scale claim. Table 2 reports TimesNet anomaly-detection F1 = 0.487, while Table 7 reports the same task for TimesNet as 0.462 (without scale) and 0.740 (with scale); root-cause TimesNet is 0.685 in Table 4 vs 0.688→0.756 in Table 7. The relationship between the main benchmark setup and the base/scale-aware variants is never explained, so the central 'scale matters' result cannot be verified as reported.

The scale insight is essentially a post-hoc application of the NME trick (Lin et al., 2024), so it is not a novel finding, and the specific claim that scale is critical for location estimation is not demonstrated — Table 7 location gains are marginal (~1 point), and the argument that magnitudes 'encode distance-related properties' is speculative rather than tested.

Heavy dependence on LLM-generated supervision with weak validation. Troubleshooting tickets, anomaly parameter ranges, and reasoning traces are generated by LLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen3-32B, GPT-o3), conditioned on ground-truth labels, and filtered only by a hand-designed regex/heuristic scoring function; there is no human evaluation of trace faithfulness, and conditioning on ground truth raises leakage concerns for downstream reasoning training/evaluation.

Much of the Q&A is template-generated from computed statistics and metadata (mean, variance, FFT periodicity, linear-regression trend), yielding 2.2M low-difficulty instances; the example in Appendix E even shows a 'reasoning' field for a variance question, contradicting the stated design that time-series QA requires no reasoning. This inflates dataset size without a clear reasoning contribution.

Generalizability is overstated. Data come from a single lab testbed, one base station, one UE, one band (n78), and a handful of applications; the claim that this 'supports generalizability beyond the testbed setting' is not substantiated, and synthetic anomalies dominate the anomaly set, making the distribution far from real operational observability data.

Evaluation rigor is limited: anomaly detection uses a single random 1,000-sample subset with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, and the narrative is mixed (e.g., Mantis F1 = 0.800, Toto root-cause accuracy = 0.848, near-perfect network QA), which does not cleanly support the claim that state-of-the-art models 'consistently struggle.'

Dataset scale is modest relative to the 'large-scale' framing (32K samples × 128 steps); 'millions of observations' is technically true but small for foundation-model pretraining, and no comparison against a normalized version of the same data is provided for the main tasks to isolate the normalization effect.

Failure analysis is thin: a single illustrative false-positive case (Fig. 6) is used to explain model failures, with no systematic breakdown by anomaly type, KPI, or error mode, and no ablation of the LLM-as-input serialization choices used to feed time series to language models.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: observability data is scarce in public benchmarks due to proprietary/privacy restrictions, and TelecomTS provides a de-anonymized, scale-preserving alternative that prior work (e.g., BOOM) does not.

The data collection methodology is unusually detailed and reproducible: a real standalone 5G network (OAI stack, USRP N300/X310, 18 KPIs at 100 ms), controlled jamming, three spatial zones, static/mobile profiles, and congestion scenarios, with explicit system-level tuning to stabilize measurements.

Anomaly curation is principled rather than arbitrary: real jamming-induced anomalies are combined with ten literature-grounded synthetic anomaly types, exponential-duration modeling, KPI-boundary handling, and human-in-the-loop validation of tickets and parameters.

The dataset supports a broad, useful task suite (anomaly detection, duration localization, root cause analysis, forecasting, time series Q&A, network-level Q&A) with reasoning traces, going beyond the forecasting-only focus of most prior datasets.

The scale ablation (Table 7) is a valuable and cleanly designed contribution, showing consistent gains (up to 30-41 points for Autoformer) when absolute-scale NME features are added, supporting the paper's core motivation about normalization obscuring diagnostic magnitude information.

The benchmarking is broad, covering LLMs, reasoning models, TS foundation models, classic TS architectures, and a multi-modal model, giving a useful snapshot of current capabilities on observability data.

The comparison in Appendix A (ETTh1, MotorImagery, FRED-MD, WTH) effectively substantiates the claim that existing multivariate datasets are homogeneous, temporally/spatially aggregated, and lack categorical variates.
weaknesses: The central narrative that 'existing approaches consistently struggle' is overstated relative to the evidence. Mantis reaches 0.800 F1 on anomaly detection and Toto reaches 0.921 F1 on anomaly duration, indicating that scale-aware and observability-pretrained models handle substantial portions of the benchmark well. The framing should be more calibrated.

The forecasting results (Table 5) contain a large, unexplained inconsistency: classic models (Informer 0.143, TimesNet 0.159, per-KPI linear regression 0.162) dramatically outperform all foundation models (Moment 0.543, Moirai2 0.516, Toto 0.489, Mantis 0.457). A ~3-5x MAE gap of this kind usually signals a protocol/scaling discrepancy and needs explicit clarification (e.g., normalization, per-channel vs. aggregated error, prediction horizon).

Reasoning traces are synthesized by an LLM conditioned on ground-truth labels and task metadata. Even with blacklist-based leakage constraints, this raises concerns about whether traces reflect faithful reasoning or post-hoc rationalization, which matters given the paper positions them as supervision/evaluation signals for reasoning and RL.

Synthetic anomalies are partly generated and validated via GPT-4.1, and fidelity to real-world faults is asserted but not quantitatively validated (e.g., no distributional comparison between synthetic and real anomalies, or expert study beyond informal 'human feedback').
Anomaly detection is evaluated on only 1,000 randomly selected samples; the paper does not report variance or sensitivity to this subsampling, so the stability of the reported metrics is unclear.

The multi-modal model (Toto+Qwen-3-4B) is the authors' own and is trained on TelecomTS, so its consistent advantage on network Q&A is partly expected and not compared against a strong, matched external multi-modal baseline. Reporting only best/worst-KPI MAE (Table 6) also makes the time series Q&A comparison hard to interpret.

Generalizability is limited: a single base station, one band (n78), a ~70 m^2 lab, and synthetic-only coverage for most fault categories. The claim that the setup 'supports generalizability of our dataset beyond the testbed setting' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility/presentation issues: the abstract's code link is truncated ('The code is available at:'), and several reported Q&A counts (64 time series categories, 2.2M instances) appear inflated by templated generation, which should be clarified to avoid overstating dataset richness.
Reasoning-trace quality is assessed only via an automatic scoring function; no human evaluation is reported, so the claimed faithfulness of traces (Figure 17) rests on LLM-based scoring alone.
